The difficulty with discussing tax policy is everybody has a different definition of 'rich' and people greatly misunderstand the bracket system used in US tax law.

It is impossible to compare rates from decade to decade because the tax brackets are very different now than they were 20, 30, or 50 years ago.

Currently a man making $500,000 a year, a man making $1 million a year, a man making $20 million year, and a man making $120 million a year are all in the same tax bracket. I ask you is this fair?

Compare this with a man making $20,000 a year, a man making $30,000, and a man making $60,000 a year are all in a different tax bracket.

This upside down tax bracket system is largely the result of Ronald Reagan and trickle down economics. Carter began reducing the number tax brackets, Reagan reduced this number even further, and Bush even further. Clinton increase the number of tax brackets slightly in an attempt to raise more revenue and Bush decrease the number again with the Bush era tax cuts. Resulting in a tax system in which the middle-class pays more percent of their income then the higher class.

Secondly, the tax code indicates your marginal tax rate whereas most politicians cite effective tax rates as well as marginal tax rates depending on which is most convenient to support their argument.

For those who do not know your marginal tax rate is the tax rate which is listed in 26 USC 1. Your marginal tax rate is calculated per individual dollar. For example, if you earn $50,000 a year you pay 15% on the first $36,900 ($5,535), and 28% on the remaining $13,100 ($3,660). Meaning your total tax bill would be $9,203.

The point being it is extremely difficult to make comparisons of tax policy decade to decade.
